value.overview: The Bay Wren (Cantorchilus nigricapillus) is a small, active songbird of humid tropical forests in southern Central America and northwestern South America. It is recognized by its dark crown, pale cheek markings, rich rufous-brown back, and strongly barred wings and tail. Usually encountered in dense vegetation rather than in the open, it often reveals its presence through a loud, repeated song. In Costa Rica, it is a characteristic wren of humid Caribbean lowland forests.
value.classification: The Bay Wren belongs to the wren family Troglodytidae and the genus Cantorchilus. Several geographically distinct subspecies are recognized across its range, including forms occurring in Costa Rica.
value.identification: The Bay Wren is about 13–14 cm long. It has rufous-brown upperparts, a predominantly blackish crown and face, contrasting white or pale buff ear coverts, and a white throat. The wings and tail are barred, while the lowerparts vary geographically from whitish to buffy or more heavily marked. Its long, slightly curved bill and habit of moving quickly through tangled vegetation help distinguish it from many other Costa Rican wrens. Its loud, rolling song is often easier to detect than the bird itself.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from eastern Nicaragua through Costa Rica and Panama to northwestern South America, including parts of Colombia and Ecuador. In Costa Rica it is principally associated with the humid Caribbean slope and adjacent lowlands, including forests around Sarapiquí, Limón, and other wet northeastern and southeastern regions. It inhabits mature and second-growth evergreen forest, forest edges, dense understory, vine tangles, and vegetation near streams. It is generally a lowland bird but may occur into foothill elevations where conditions remain humid.
value.migrationStatus: The Bay Wren is considered a resident species. Individuals in Costa Rica are present year-round, with no regular long-distance migration known.
value.breeding: Bay Wrens form territorial pairs and breed in humid forest habitats. The nest is a domed or globular structure made from plant fibers, leaves, and other vegetation, with a side entrance. It is usually placed low or moderately high in dense vegetation, vines, or tangled branches. Both adults are believed to participate in nest building and care of the young. Breeding activity may vary with local rainfall, and detailed information on clutch size and nesting success remains limited.
value.dietFeeding: The Bay Wren feeds mainly on insects and other small invertebrates, including beetles, ants, caterpillars, spiders, and similar prey. It searches methodically through dense understory, leaf litter, vines, fallen vegetation, and low branches, often moving with quick hops and short flights. Its slender bill is well suited to probing crevices and turning through foliage. Foraging birds may remain concealed even when calling frequently.
value.behavior: This wren is energetic, secretive, and strongly territorial. It usually travels through pairs or family groups in dense vegetation and often keeps close to the ground or middle levels of the understory. The song is loud and repetitive, and paired birds may answer one another or call while moving through their territory. Bay Wrens commonly flick or raise the tail as they forage and may investigate intruders with sharp calls.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not well quantified. The species remains locally common in suitable habitat, although habitat loss may be causing gradual declines in parts of its range.
